opus-5.5.text:
What strikes me most about Noam is how intuitive his understanding is. A lot of us in the field reason about models empirically: we run an experiment, look at the curves, and adjust. Noam seems to have an internal picture of what's happening inside the network, how information flows, where the bottlenecks are, what the hardware is actually doing. That lets him make leaps that look surprising from the outside but feel almost obvious to him.

He's also unusual in thinking about the model and the compute together. Many researchers treat the hardware as a given and focus on the math. Noam asks what kind of architecture makes the best use of the accelerators we actually have. You can see that thread in a lot of the ideas associated with him: attention mechanisms that parallelize well, mixture-of-experts approaches that scale capacity without scaling compute proportionally, and tweaks that make inference cheaper. Those aren't just elegant ideas. They're shaped by a deep sense of what will work at scale.

And he has great taste in simplicity. Often his contributions are small changes, a different activation function or a different way of sharing keys and values, that turn out to matter a lot. Knowing which small change is worth trying, out of the thousands you could try, is a rare skill. That combination of intuition, systems awareness, and a willingness to keep things simple is what I find most impressive.

fable-5.1.text:
Noam has this almost physical intuition for what's happening inside a model, and that's the part that always got me. Most of us, when we're trying to figure out why something isn't training well or why a model is behaving a certain way, we go to the data. We run the experiments, we look at the loss curves, we try a dozen ablations. Noam would look at the architecture and the math and just tell you, "this part is going to be a bottleneck," or "this attention head doesn't need to be that wide," and then you'd go run it and he'd be right.

I remember when we were working together at Google Brain, he had this way of thinking about the whole system at once. Not just the model, but the hardware it ran on, how the memory bandwidth constrained what the model could actually compute per step, what that meant for the design. Mixture of experts is a good example. A lot of people had the vague idea that you'd want to route to specialized sub-networks, but he understood exactly why it would be efficient on TPUs, where the communication costs would show up, and how to make the gating actually train. That's not a paper-reading kind of understanding. That's an engineer who has really built things and watched them break.

And the other thing is he's unusually unsentimental about ideas, including his own. If something was elegant but didn't help, he dropped it. If something was ugly but worked, he'd keep it and then figure out why it worked. He thinks in terms of what the model actually needs to learn the function, not what looks nice in a diagram. Honestly, a lot of what became standard in transformers came from that mindset, and I think people underestimate how rare it is.

It’s one thing to have a high-level idea about why a neural network should work; it’s another to think through what that means for the architecture, the training process, and the computation involved. That combination—seeing the big picture while being able to reason carefully about the mechanics—is what I find particularly impressive.
